title: Chasing clients for missing documents on Mac: a weekly routine for accountants in 2026
metaTitle: Chasing clients for missing documents: a Mac routine for accountants
description: Chasing clients for missing documents takes real hours each week. Here is what it costs, why it keeps happening, and fixes you can run on a Mac today.
intro: Chasing clients for missing documents means following up until the paperwork you need actually arrives. On a Mac, most of that time comes back when you send one exact request, collect files in one place, and track every open item in one sheet. This page covers what the chase costs, why it keeps happening, and fixes you can use without buying anything.
tldr: Survey numbers vary, but many accounting teams spend days per engagement gathering client information.
Clients forget items, send mixed formats, and get vague requests. Fix the request before you chase harder.
Write one exact checklist per client, send it once, and track each item in a Numbers or Excel sheet.
Use one upload link for files, and set a reminder date for every missing item.
Lazur can draft reminders, point at buttons, and walk you through QuickBooks steps. It does not send or click for you.

blocks.text: What the chase looks like in a normal week

Most of the chase is not one big email. It is a loop. You send a request, wait, check what came back, find the gaps, and ask again. Each round trip costs a few minutes of reading and a few minutes of writing. The loop repeats for every client, every engagement, and every missing page.

The loop breaks down in predictable places. The request was vague, so the client sent the wrong year. The file arrived as a phone photo, so you asked again for a PDF. The client forgot the second account, and nobody noticed until the file was nearly done. Each break adds a round trip, and each round trip adds waiting.
How much time chasing clients really takes

Nobody has measured this cleanly across the whole profession. The best numbers come from software companies and consultants who sell to accountants, so each figure has a commercial interest behind it. Read them as signals, not audits.

The CPA Practice Advisor and Canopy survey of 240 accounting professionals is the most specific. Of those surveyed, 49% said they typically spend 1 to 2 days communicating with clients to gather information for a standard engagement. Another 36% said 3 to 7 days, and 16% said two weeks or more.

A 2026 survey of 355 firms across ten industries, reported by Dynamic Business, puts collection and chasing at close to 20 hours a week. That survey covers many industries, not only accounting, so treat it as a rough guide for your firm. The same survey reports a median of roughly US$60,000 a year in nonbillable work.

Financial Cents sells practice-management software, and its 2025 report says getting documents from clients is still the biggest workflow issue. Its platform data shows clients take an average of 5 days to submit requested documents. That is data from its own users, so it shows the pattern, not the whole market.
Write a request clients can finish in one pass

Most follow-ups happen because the first request was unclear. A client reads 'send your statements' and sends whatever they happen to have. The fix is to name each item the way your accounting software names it, with a period and an account.

items: List every item by name, period, and account, such as 'Bank statement, business checking, January to March'.
Say the format you need, such as a PDF downloaded from the bank, not a phone photo.
Give one due date for everything, and say what happens if an item is late.
Give one place to send files, not three options.
Say what to do if an item does not exist, such as a one-line reply that says so.

blocks.text: Keep the message short enough to read on a phone. Clients often read requests between meetings. A long list tends to get a reply to the first few bullets, and the rest waits for a second email.

Save the request as a reusable message so you do not rewrite it for every client. Outlook supports saved templates for this. The [Outlook for accountants page](/for/accountants/outlook) has ideas for setting up templates and flags.
Track every item in one Numbers or Excel sheet

A tracker turns a memory problem into a list you can check. One row per missing item is the simplest setup. Filter for anything still marked missing before each client call, and you will know what to ask for first.

In Numbers on Mac, add a table with the Table button, then name your columns in the header row. [How to add a table in Numbers](/how-to/add-a-table-in-numbers) covers the steps. For a fuller setup, see [Numbers for accountants on Mac](/for/accountants/numbers).

rows: Client name and the contact who answers
One row per client, so reminders reach the right person
Exact document name, period, and account
Vague items cause a second request
Shows how long the item has been open
Keeps follow-ups on a schedule, not in your head
Flags files that need to be sent again
Lets you filter for what still blocks the file
blocks.caption: A starting tracker for one engagement. Copy the headers, then add your own rows.

blocks.text: Keep one engagement per tab or sheet. A single sheet for every client becomes hard to scan by the second busy week. Old rows are easy to forget, so mark items received or not needed instead of deleting them.
Use one upload link instead of email attachments

Email is where documents go to get lost. Attachments pile up in one inbox, and size limits or password prompts create extra trips. A single upload link puts every file in one folder, with the names you asked for.

Dropbox file requests let anyone send files to you without a Dropbox account. File requests are available on all Dropbox plans. Basic, Plus, and Family customers can request files up to 2 GB. Basic and Plus accounts cannot set a deadline or allow late uploads, so check your plan first.

To make one, open File requests in the Dropbox web sidebar and click New request. Add a title and description, choose a destination folder, and optionally add a password. Click Create, then enter the client emails or copy the link.

Check your firm's rules on client data before you send any upload link. In the CPA Practice Advisor survey, 49% of professionals said clients may email sensitive information such as tax forms. The other 51% do not allow it. Your firm's policy decides which method you use.
Set reminders that get a reply

Reminders work, but the strongest evidence comes from other fields. A megastudy of 47,306 primary-care patients tested text messages sent before a visit. The average effect was about a 5% boost in vaccination rates.

A review of 126 randomized trials covering 23 million people found the average nudge-unit effect was 1.4 percentage points, an 8.0% increase. Those effects are small. Small gains still matter when you send the same reminder to every client.

For your own follow-ups, keep the schedule simple. Send the request, send one reminder when the deadline is close, and call about anything still missing after the deadline. Write the next date in the tracker before you close the email.
Attach bank statements in QuickBooks Online without the hunt

When a client sends a bank statement, the most useful home for it is the bank reconciliation. A 2023 answer in the Intuit QuickBooks Community gives the path. Check it against your own version before you train anyone on it.

items: Go to Transactions > Reconcile, then open History by account.
Pick the account and the statement period.
Drag in the file or choose it, then click Done.

blocks.text: A 2020 Intuit reply says this feature needs QuickBooks Online Plus, Advanced, Accountant, or QuickBooks Live, and that the bank must be connected. Those details may have changed. Check the current Intuit help for your plan before you rely on them.
Auto-file client downloads with Hazel

If clients send links or your portal drops PDFs into Downloads, the folder fills fast. Hazel, a Mac app from Noodlesoft, can watch a folder and file each download by rule. It is a separate app you install.

In Hazel, use Folder > Add App Folder to watch the download location of an installed browser. Chrome, Safari, and Firefox save to Downloads by default, and the Hazel entry follows your browser's download setting. Adding the folder does nothing on its own. You still need rules that sort the files.
Start with one rule. Move files whose names contain a client name into that client's folder, and test it on a few files first. A rule that moves the wrong file is worse than no rule at all.
Hubdoc on Mac: check before you rely on it

Hubdoc is a Xero product for collecting bills and statements. Its Mac App Store listing, version 6.6.6 from 2025, requires macOS 12.0 or later and an Apple M1 chip or later. The app is free to download.

The listing averages 2.2 out of 5 from 13 ratings. It also says 'Designed for iPad. Not verified for macOS.' Treat the Mac app as a weak option. If your firm uses Hubdoc, test the web version in Chrome first.
Mistakes that make chasing take longer

items: Sending five short emails instead of one full list. Each email starts a thread the client has to match up.
Asking for 'everything' without naming items. Clients guess, and guesses come back wrong.
Accepting phone photos without checking that every page is readable and complete.
Chasing by phone only. A call leaves no written list of what was asked.
Forgetting to record the date you asked. Without it, you cannot tell which item is overdue.
Sending client files through a personal email or chat app. Check your firm's rules first.

blocks.text: What to do when a client never sends the document

Some items never arrive. Set a cutoff date, then send one final note that says what you will do without the item. That might be an estimate, an extension, or a note in the file. Pick the option your firm uses for missing items, and write the decision in the tracker.
Password-protected PDFs need their own step. Ask for the password in a separate message, not in the same email, or ask for an unprotected copy. Your firm's policy decides which method is allowed.

blocks.title: Client data rules
blocks.text: Follow your employer's rules for client data before you use email, upload links, or AI tools on any client file. Rules differ between firms, and regulated work can have strict ones.
Where Lazur fits, and where it does not

Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac. You hold a key and talk. It can see your screen while you hold the shortcut, point at things, answer out loud, and draft or type text. It does not click buttons or operate other apps for you.

For this problem, Lazur helps most with the steps you repeat. It can show you where a button lives, walk through a QuickBooks path, draft a reminder you review, and take dictated notes. It does not decide which client to chase or when a file counts as complete.

Privacy matters here. Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer you, and they are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models. Your firm's rules still come first.
Lazur has a free trial that needs no credit card. Check [pricing](/pricing) for plans and limits, and [download Lazur](/download) when you want to try it on your Mac.

faq.question: What is the fastest way to start chasing clients for missing documents?
faq.answer: Stop chasing from memory. Write an exact list of items for each client, send it once, and record the date you asked. Then check the tracker each week and send a reminder only for items still open. The list does most of the work.

faq.question: How often should I send reminders?
faq.answer: Send the first request, one reminder when the deadline is close, and a call or final note for anything still missing after the deadline. Write the next date in your tracker before closing each email. A fixed schedule beats a reminder you send only when you remember.

faq.question: Is it okay to chase clients by text message?
faq.answer: Text reminders have modest evidence behind them, and that evidence comes from patient vaccination and similar studies, not accounting. Check your firm's rules on texting clients and on sending client details by text before you use it.

faq.question: Should I accept phone photos of statements?
faq.answer: Accept them only when every page is readable and complete. An Accounting Today opinion piece lists phone snapshots and password-protected PDFs among common problems with client submissions. Ask for a PDF in your request if you need one.

faq.question: Can I use Dropbox file requests for every client?
faq.answer: Dropbox says file requests are on all plans, and recipients do not need a Dropbox account. Basic and Plus accounts cannot set deadlines or allow late uploads, and file size is capped at 2 GB on those plans. Check your plan and your firm's data rules first.

faq.question: Does Lazur send my client files anywhere?
faq.answer: Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers so they can answer you, and they are not stored. Your employer's rules for client data still decide whether you can use it on client files.

faq.question: Does Lazur click the buttons in QuickBooks for me?
faq.answer: No. Lazur guides you one click at a time and waits for each click. It can also circle a button on your screen so you can find it. You do the clicking, and you check every attachment yourself.

faq.question: What if a client never sends the document?
faq.answer: Set a cutoff date and send one final note that says what you will do without the item. Your firm may allow an estimate, an extension, or a note in the file. Record the decision in the tracker so the file has a clear history.

How accounting firms can spend less time managing client documents

costs.title: Days added to each engagement
costs.text: Survey data suggests the wait is often the real cost. In a 2024 survey, 36% of accounting professionals said gathering client information takes 3 to 7 days per standard engagement, and 16% said two weeks or more. Each day of waiting pushes the rest of the work back, even when the staff hours look small.

costs.title: Staff hours that never reach a bill
costs.text: A 2026 survey of 355 firms reports close to 20 hours a week spent on collecting documents and chasing clients. That figure covers several industries, so it is a rough guide. The same survey puts the median nonbillable cost at roughly US$60,000 a year. Check how many hours your own team loses before you decide what to fix first.

costs.title: Risk from the wrong channel
costs.text: When a client cannot find a clean upload route, they often send files by ordinary email. In one 2024 survey, 49% of accounting professionals allowed clients to email sensitive information such as tax forms. Sensitive files in the wrong place create a data problem that is much harder to fix than a late statement.

costs.title: Burnout that is hard to measure
costs.text: Survey writers link document chasing to burnout, since the work is repetitive and interrupts other tasks. The burnout figures I found come from software vendors and secondary coverage, so treat them as a signal, not a measurement. Still, the daily nagging is real, and it lands on the people who already carry the busiest season.

causes.title: Clients forget what you asked for
causes.text: A request sent once in a long email is easy to miss. Clients are busy, and they often answer the parts they remember. Without a written list and a date, the missing item stays missing until someone notices it weeks later.

causes.title: Requests are vague
causes.text: 'Send your statements' can mean five different files to five different people. Clients guess, and guesses come back as the wrong year, the wrong account, or a summary instead of the statement. Vague requests create the second and third rounds of chasing.

causes.title: Files arrive in the wrong format
causes.text: An Accounting Today opinion piece lists disorganized intake, password-protected PDFs, phone snapshots, and unsorted statements as common problems. The piece is opinion and gives no measured data. Still, the pattern matches what most preparers see: a photo of a page is not a statement.

causes.title: Submitting is harder than it should be
causes.text: The same opinion piece argues that complicated submission steps push clients toward email. A client who cannot find the upload page sends the file to the first address they remember. That habit moves sensitive data outside the systems your firm meant to use.

causes.title: No one owns the open list
causes.text: When reminders live in memory, follow-ups happen at random. Some items get three reminders and others get none. A tracker with a next-reminder date gives every open item an owner and a date, so the chase has a shape.

fixes.title: Write one exact checklist per client type
fixes.text: Make a short list for each kind of client, such as a sole trader, a landlord, or a payroll-only client. Name every item by its period and account, and say the format you need. Reuse the list for the next season. Edit it when you see the same gap twice, and the list gets better each year.

fixes.title: Send one request, not five emails
fixes.text: Put the full list, the single upload link, and the due date in one message. Save it as a reusable message in Outlook so you can send it fast. When something is missing later, reply in the same thread, so the client sees the whole history in one place.

fixes.title: Give clients one upload place
fixes.text: Use one folder or one file request link for every document. Dropbox file requests let people send files without an account, and Basic and Plus accounts can request files up to 2 GB each. Check your firm's data rules before you use any upload link with client files.

fixes.title: Set reminder dates and keep them
fixes.text: Write a next-reminder date next to every open item. Send one reminder when the deadline is close and one final note after it passes. The evidence for reminders is modest and comes from other fields, but a fixed schedule costs you little and keeps the chase orderly.

fixes.title: Track open items in one sheet
fixes.text: Build a tracker in Numbers or Excel with one row per missing item. Filter for Missing before each client call. Keep one engagement per tab, and mark items received instead of deleting them, so the history stays intact for the reviewer.

fixes.title: Send downloads to the right folder with Hazel
fixes.text: If clients send links or you download files often, install Hazel and add the browser download folder with Folder > Add App Folder. Adding the folder does nothing until you add rules, so write one rule for each client folder and test it on a few files before you trust it.

fixes.title: Attach statements where they belong
fixes.text: In QuickBooks Online, attach each bank statement to the reconciliation through Transactions > Reconcile > History by account. Check the path on your version first. Attaching the file to the reconciliation keeps it with the work that needs it, not in someone's downloads folder.

plan.label: Before
plan.title: Write the checklist once
plan.text: Build one exact list for each client type. Name each item by period and account, and say the format you need. Save the list as a reusable message so you can send it without rewriting.

plan.label: Monday
plan.title: Send one request per client
plan.text: Send the full list, the upload link, and the due date in one message. Record the date you asked in the tracker. Each open item gets its own row with a status and a next reminder date.

plan.label: Wednesday
plan.title: Check the tracker and reply to gaps
plan.text: Filter the tracker for Missing. Reply in the same thread for each gap, and name the exact item again. Send a reminder for anything with a deadline that is close.

plan.label: Friday
plan.title: Escalate what blocks the file
plan.text: Call the client about items that still block the work. Send a final note for anything past the cutoff, and write what you will do without it. Update the status column before the call ends.

plan.label: Weekly
plan.title: Clear the tracker and set next dates
plan.text: Mark received items, remove duplicates, and set a next-reminder date for every open row. Note which client caused the most follow-ups, and update that client's checklist.
